newsitem.title: USA: Sears reaches pacts in credit card dispute.
newsitem.headline: Sears reaches pacts in credit card dispute.

text.p: Sears, Roebuck and Co, seeking to put to rest a flap over its method of collecting credit card debt, said Tuesday it has reached preliminary settlements with consumers and state and federal regulators.
The agreements are still subject to negotiations and require the approval of the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Massachusetts, among others, Sears said in a court filing.

Sears said the agreements would resolve legal proceedings with consumers in several civil lawsuits, representatives for Attorneys General in 39 states, the U.S. Attorney in Massachusetts and the U.S. Federal Trade Commission.
The agreements would resolve claims that the retailer's method of collecting debt from Sears credit card holders who had filed for bankruptcy protection was illegal.

In April, Sears said it mishandled so-called reaffirmation agreements by failing to file them in bankruptcy court. The company has launched a record search to find out how many consumers are entitled to restitution.
The Hoffman Estates, Ill.,-based retailer also voluntarily offered to repay consumers who signed the mishandled agreements and to give them each a $100 gift certificate.

The company's filing was an update of settlement talks with a Massachusetts bankruptcy judge who is scheduled to hold a hearing on Thursday, June 5, at which Sears hoped to present an agreement for approval.

The retailer said it was scheduled to meet Wednesday with federal prosecutors. The U.S. Justice Department was expected to file a status report with the Massachusetts bankruptcy court on a potential criminal investigation by Thursday, according to Sears.
Sears has been scouring records between 1992 and 1997 involving 500,000 repayment agreements with credit card customers to calculate its liability.

In the court filing, Sears did not say how much the settlement would cost. It said it would identify by August 15 the number of consumers who signed the repayment agreements that were not properly filed in court.

Meanwhile, Sears said it reached an agreement in principle covering compensation, penalities and other issues with the Massachusetts attorney general, who has headed a group representing 39 states in the negotiations.
The pact was being presented to 39 attorneys general for formal approval, Sears said in the filing.
A spokesman for Massachusetts Attorney General Scott Harshbarger said the deal had not been completed. "There is not an official settlement with Sears," said spokesman John Lamontagne.
A consent order has been reached with the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, which could approve the deal Wednesday, Sears said.

But U.S. Attorney for Massachusetts Donald Stern has asked the bankruptcy court to delay any settlement Sears proposes. If a settlement were approved, it could impact Stern's pending investigation of Sears and present double-jeopardy problems for the prosecution, said spokeswoman Amy Rindskopf.

In addition to settlement costs, the U.S. Bankruptcy Court could order Sears pay punitive damages. But Sears said it could be protected against court-imposed fines by laws barring multiple government punishments for the same offense.
